# Circuit OS against real circuits — and the build check, measured

*A snapshot, frozen 2026-10-08. Every number is regenerated by the commands in §10. **Nothing here was measured on a board.** The real circuits are published designs read from their sources; the oracle is ngspice; the "wrongly built boards" are ngspice netlists. D1 (no bench measurement) is still open.*

## 1. What was asked

1. *Is what Circuit OS generates good enough, set beside real, well-designed circuits that anyone can read?*
2. *How accurate is a validator that tells a correctly built board from a wrongly built one, by physics?*

For (2) the validator described on 2026-10-06 did not exist yet, so it was built first (`backend/validation/build_check.py`), then measured.

## 2. The answer in brief

**Generated designs against real ones.** Circuit OS was asked for the same job as 11 real circuits (13 runs — the Modbus bias range is three points). It refused one and produced a design for each of the rest; every design it produced meets the criteria taken from the standards and datasheets (§4). It hits the number it is asked for to within 0.4 % on the LED, 0.3 % on the divider and 0.1 % on the RC cutoff. Where it differs from real practice, it is usually more careful (it moves the DHT22 pull-up with the cable; its divider is more accurate than SparkFun's). Four differences are worth acting on:

1. **RS-485 bias is the weakest of every published design.** 549 Ω gives an idle bus of 240 mV at the low end of the rail with 1 % parts, 40 mV over the 200 mV threshold — but TI's own worked example (523 Ω) holds 252 mV, and the generator's stated margin (250 mV) is only met at the *requested* rail, not across its ±5 %. The cause is one line of the generator (§6).
2. **The project's rule engine passes any bias value** — a bus biased through 100 kΩ passes while reading 1.7 mV (§7).
3. **The envelope refuses dim indicator LEDs** that real boards use (the Feather's 0.66 mA is below its 1 mA floor).
4. **A divider always bleeds about 0.5 mA**, and the form has no field to change it: a real battery monitor uses 21 µA.

**The build check.** On 2,400 simulated correct boards per reading set it never accused one. On 4,760 simulated wrong boards it noticed every one and, when it named a fault, never named the wrong one. Naming the *exact* fault depends on what is measured: **voltages alone name it 36 % of the time even if every voltage is read; adding three to six power-off resistance readings names it 85 % of the time (92.5 % on the real circuits).** A short plan notices a fault with 1–4 readings; a plan that also names it takes 3–6. The guarantee it states was attacked with 13,500 adversarial readings (every corner of the faulty board's tolerance box, three rail values, meter error pushed as far toward the design as its accuracy allows) with **zero violations**. The part it cannot see at all is a capacitor's value.

**Three calls are yours** (§9): whether a resistance that reads off should keep D1 closed (I made it so; one property to flip), whether to size the RS-485 bias at the rail's low end, and whether the form gets a bleed-current field and a lower LED floor.

## 3. The real circuits

Eleven, each read from its source on 2026-10-08. They were read by the agent; **no person has verified them** (the standing `data/figures.py` records have before `scripts/verify_figures.py`). Evidence classes, strongest first: **EAGLE netlist** (the vendor's own `.sch`, parsed with ElementTree from the GitHub API — connectivity machine-read, nothing summarised by a model); **standard / app-note text** and **datasheet figure** (read from the document's text layer or the extracted image); **tutorial text**.

| Circuit | What it is | Source | Read as |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rs485.modbus_v102.dc_150` | Polarized pair: pull-up to 5 V and pull-down, 450–650 Ω; 150 Ω terminations | MODBUS over Serial Line V1.02 §3.4.5–3.4.6 | standard text |
| `rs485.ti_slla272d.fig7_1` | Idle-bus failsafe: R_B 523 Ω ×2, R_T 120 Ω | TI SLLA272D, *The RS-485 Design Guide* §7, Fig. 7-1 | app-note text |
| `rs485.sparkfun_breakout` | Transceiver board, 220 Ω across A–B, no bias | `sparkfun/RS-485_Breakout` `RS485_Breakout.sch` | EAGLE netlist |
| `led.feather_m0_d13` | D13 → 2.2 kΩ → red 0805 LED | `adafruit/Adafruit-Feather-M0-Basic-Proto-PCB` rev C `.sch` | EAGLE netlist |
| `led.sparkfun_rs485_rts` | RTS → 330 Ω → green 0603 LED | same SparkFun board | EAGLE netlist |
| `divider.feather_m0_vbat` | Battery monitor VBAT → 100 kΩ → D9 → 100 kΩ → GND | same Feather | EAGLE netlist |
| `divider.sparkfun_5v_to_3v3` | 1 kΩ + 2 kΩ, 5 V → 3.3 V | SparkFun *Logic Levels* tutorial | tutorial text |
| `dht22.aosong_datasheet` | DATA with a 5K pull-up to VDD | Aosong DHT22 datasheet §5 (SparkFun-hosted copy) | datasheet figure |
| `dht22.adafruit_guide` | 10 kΩ between VCC and the data pin | Adafruit *DHT* guide | tutorial text |
| `rc.nxp_an14520` | PWM-DAC filter 4.7 kΩ / 0.1 µF at 3.3 V, 40 kHz | NXP AN14520 Rev. 1.1 §2.2 | app-note text |
| `rc.espressif_en_delay` | EN-pin RC delay 10 kΩ / 1 µF | ESP Hardware Design Guidelines, *Chip Power-up and Reset Timing* | app-note text |

What was assumed where a source is silent is written in the corpus (`backend/data/reference_designs.json`, `assumed`): resistor tolerance (1 % unless stated), the LED's forward-voltage class (the project's own red 0805 figures for "RED 0805"; a conventional 2.1 V green for the 0603), the MCU pin's output resistance (40 Ω, irrelevant at these resistances), the cable's capacitance (a range, 50–100 pF/m). The AM2302-labelled copy of the Aosong datasheet carries its diagram too small to read ("1K" or "5K" — I could not tell); the SparkFun-hosted DHT22 copy is legible and is the one cited. The SparkFun board's R4 is labelled `220` in its value and `22OHM` in its device name; the value was taken, and a community thread asks whether it should be 120 Ω.

No machine-readable board with a DHT22 line, and no board netlist for a plain RC low-pass, turned up in a search of reasonable length; those two families rest on datasheets and application notes. Eleven is not a sample of the world's circuits: "none was reproduced wrongly" is the strongest thing it supports.

## 4. How "good enough" is judged

ngspice judges, never a generator's `predict()` or its claims. The criteria come from the documents, not from the generators:

| Family | Criterion | From |
|---|---|---|
| RS-485 | worst-case idle V_AB ≥ 200 mV over the rail ±5 %, 1 % parts, with and without two receivers loading the pair; also reported against TI's 250 mV worked-example target | TI SLLA272D §4, §7 |
| LED | LED current ≤ its rating; pin current ≤ 20 mA; nominal current within ±20 % of the request | ATmega328P datasheet (20 mA recommended); LED rating assumed |
| Divider | V_out within 2 % of the request; the worst case over 1 % parts reported | project target |
| DHT22 | reported, not graded: 10–90 % rise time over cable length, sink current | Aosong datasheet gives timing, not a rise-time limit |
| RC | f_c within 5 % of the request; shift under a 50 Ω source reported | project target |

## 6. What the comparison found

1. **RS-485 bias.** The generator picks "the largest equal E96 pair that keeps worst-case V_AB at least 25 % above threshold" — 250 mV. It evaluates that at the *requested* supply as a single point, with resistor tolerance only (`rs485_node.py::select` → `_bands` uses `spec.supply`). With a rail 5 % low it is 240 mV, 20 % above the threshold. TI sizes at V_bus,min = 4.75 V, and its result is the largest standard value that keeps 250 mV there. ngspice, same parts and loading:

   | R_B | 487 Ω | 511 Ω | **523 Ω** | 536 Ω | **549 Ω** (generator) | 562 Ω |
   |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
   | worst-case V_AB at 4.75 V | 269.2 mV | 257.3 mV | **251.7 mV** | 245.9 mV | **240.4 mV** | 235.1 mV |

   The design does clear the receiver threshold; nothing here says it fails. It does not meet the margin its own docstring states, at the rail's low end. Sizing at `supply × 0.95` gives 523 Ω. I have not changed the generator: a bias value changes every RS-485 design it produces.
2. **Dim indicators.** A 0.66 mA indicator (the Feather's D13) is refused: `led_current_ma=0.66 outside 1–20 mA`. Real boards use currents that low.
3. **Divider bleed.** The generator picks about 10 kΩ total whatever the use. For the Feather's battery monitor that is 498 µA against the real design's 21 µA, 24× the drain; its output impedance (2.1 kΩ) is better for an ADC than the real 50 kΩ. The generator supports a bleed-current preference; the form has no field for it.
4. **DHT22 follows the cable.** At 0.3–1 m it picks 10 kΩ (Adafruit's value, twice Aosong's 5K); at 3 m 6.98 kΩ; at 10 m 2.15 kΩ, where a fixed 10 kΩ takes 11–22 µs to rise and 2.15 kΩ takes 2.4–4.8 µs. The price is sink current: 2.3 mA at 10 m.
5. **What matched.** LED current within 0.4 % of the request (330 Ω and 365 Ω differ because the LED model and the pin's resistance differ); divider error 0.26 % against SparkFun's 1.0 %; the RC cutoff exact, with a higher resistance (10 kΩ against NXP's 4.7 kΩ) that halves the shift under a 50 Ω source; and for the EN network Circuit OS produced Espressif's own parts, 10 kΩ and 1 µF, even though that is below the form's 100 Hz hint.

## 7. The project's own RS-485 rules, run on the real circuits

`validation/rule_engine.py` judges an RS-485 bus from the netlist alone: a resistor between A and B (a warning outside 100–150 Ω, an error if absent), a pull-up on A and a pull-down on B (an error for each that is missing). Each real design was written as a CircuitIR by `scripts/rule_engine_on_real.py` and the rules run; beside it, the idle voltage ngspice gives.

| Design | Rule engine says | Idle V_AB, worst case |
|---|---|---:|
| Modbus V1.02, bias 450 / 550 / 650 Ω | passes | 356.7 / 295.8 / 252.8 mV |
| TI SLLA272D Fig. 7-1 | passes | 251.7 mV |
| SparkFun breakout | error: no pull-up on A; error: no pull-down on B; warning: 220 Ω outside 100–150 Ω | 0.0 mV |
| Circuit OS, generated | passes | 240.4 mV |
| **Synthetic, not from any source:** the Modbus circuit with 100 kΩ bias | **passes** | **1.7 mV** |

It agrees with the physics on every real circuit. It cannot tell a bias that holds the bus from one that does not, because it checks that a resistor exists, not how large it is. For designs a generator makes this does not matter — the generator's own claims prove the magnitude — but it would for a circuit a person supplies.

## 8. The build check

**What it is.** Given a design's netlist and the tolerance boxes the proofs already use, it: lists the ways a build goes wrong (a part missing, a solder bridge, a value far off, two parts exchanged, a lead one hole over, an LED backwards); for every reading a multimeter can take — **power off: the resistance between two nets; power on: a voltage to ground or between two nodes** — computes the exact range the correct build can give and the same for each fault; chooses a smallest set of readings that *notices* every detectable fault (the **detect plan**) and a smallest set that also *tells apart* every pair of faults any reading can (the **identify plan**); lists the **blind spots**, each with its reason; and turns a person's readings into a verdict: `as_designed`, `inconclusive`, `fault` (naming the fault, or the suspects the readings cannot separate), or `unexplained`. The sheets for the five standard designs are in `docs/BUILD_CHECK_SHEETS.md`; `scripts/build_check_cli.py diagnose` turns typed-in readings into a verdict.

**The guarantee, narrowly.** Parts in their boxes, the rail in the range it was read in, the meter within its stated accuracy: a fault the plan detects cannot give readings the correct build could give. A separation is decided at the rail's low, middle and high ends; every one claimed was re-checked at 41 rails across the range (790 voltage separations on the 15 designs, no exception), and a test keeps doing so. The device models are assumed right; faults nobody listed are not covered; a capacitor's value is invisible to every reading. A resistor wrong by less than 1.5× is not a listed fault; the check reports how close it can see instead (below).

**Its arithmetic, checked against ngspice.** 48,368 ngspice evaluations — every corner of every tolerance box for every hypothesis and reading (29,960) and random interior points (18,408) — against the interval the check claims: the corners hit the endpoints and no interior point fell outside (`scripts/build_check_oracle.py`). This is what lets "the extremes sit at the corners" be believed.

**Its accuracy, measured.** For each of the 15 designs (the five generated, and ten of the real circuits — the SparkFun board has nothing to power), every listed fault was built 20 times in ngspice with parts drawn uniformly inside their boxes, the rail inside its range, and the meter's error inside its stated accuracy (a 3½-digit hand meter: ±(0.5 % + 3 digits) on volts, ±(0.8 % + 3 digits) on ohms, 10 MΩ input); the check was given only what a person would read. 250 listed faults, 12,900 and 13,500 adversarial replays, as below.

**Reading the numbers.**

- *The guarantee held.* No correct board was accused (0 of 2,400, for each of four reading sets), no wrong board was missed (0 of 4,760), and when the check named a fault the true one was never absent from the names. The 12,900 and 13,500 adversarial readings found no violation. Under its stated assumptions this is mathematics the experiment confirms — the informative figures are the next two.
- *Naming a fault is a matter of what is measured.* Voltage alone: 11.7 % exact with the short plan, 36.0 % even when every voltage is read — a two-node divider cannot tell R1 missing from R2 shorted by voltage. With power-off ohms: 84.6 % exact on the identify plan (3 readings for the divider, RC and DHT22, which name every fault; 6 for the LED and the full RS-485 board, whose remaining pairs no single reading is guaranteed to tell apart).
- *Blind spots fall from 42 to 12*, and the 12 are all capacitor values. A voltmeter cannot see a pull-up's value, a short through the bypass capacitor, or a shorted resistor in a filter; the ohmmeter can.
- *Outside the guarantee.* Parts twice as loose as stated, or a meter twice as inaccurate, make 9–12 % of correct boards read "a part is off" — which is true of the first and a nuisance for the second — and **none was charged to the model** (0.2 % for the bad meter). A wrong board with one part 1.25× or 0.8× its value, which is *not* a listed fault, was charged to D1 in 63 % of builds with voltages alone (and missed in 37 %); with ohms it was charged in 0 %, and in 99.4 % the check said which part reads off. Two faults at once are named one of the two 53 % of the time with voltages alone; with ohms, 99.6 % say "a part is off".
- *How far off must a resistor be?* The identify plan tells a divider's R1 or R2 once it is 5 % off, and a DHT22's pull-up likewise (by ohms; by voltage it is invisible). `Analysis.min_detectable_factor` gives the figure for any part and plan.

## 9. What is not claimed, and what is yours to decide

- **Nothing was measured on a board.** The "real data" is real designs; the readings are simulated. A bench session (`docs/BENCH_D1.md`) is the only thing that closes D1, and would turn every "simulated" here into a measurement.
- Meter model: the data-sheet accuracy of a generic 3½-digit meter. A coarser or finer meter gives a different table; `Meter(...)` takes any.
- The tolerance boxes are the proofs' — datasheet figures nobody has yet verified (D7). The supply is an ideal source; a short across it is judged by the ohmmeter, not by a sagging rail. Faults are single, or (in the stress runs) double. The parts' distribution inside their boxes is uniform, which puts more of them near the limits than a real batch does.
- **What it can fault.** Resistors, capacitors and LEDs/diodes only. A mistake at an IC's pins (A and B swapped at a transceiver), a transistor's legs, a connector, the load or the MCU is not listed and not covered; on the load switch it lists faults for R1 and C1 and nothing else. A swapped A/B pair is one of the commonest RS-485 mistakes, and a bench test (not this check) is what finds it.
- The corpus is eleven circuits, read by the agent, not yet checked by a person.
- **Your calls.** (1) `Verdict.reopens_d1` keeps D1 closed when a power-off resistance reads off. You chose "reopen D1 as today"; the status is still `unexplained` as before, and `bench.py` is untouched, but I refined *when it counts as a model question* — flip one property to restore "as today" exactly. (2) Whether to size the RS-485 bias at the rail's low end (523 Ω). (3) Whether to add a bleed-current field to the form and lower the envelope's 1 mA floor.

## 10. Reproduce

```bash
python scripts/real_data_check.py --json docs/real_data_check_2026-10-08.json   # §5, §6
python scripts/rule_engine_on_real.py                                            # §7
python scripts/build_check_oracle.py                                             # §8, the arithmetic against ngspice
python scripts/build_check_accuracy.py --trials 20 --kinds v   --json v.json     # §8, voltage readings only
python scripts/build_check_accuracy.py --trials 20 --kinds v,r --json vr.json    # §8, with power-off resistance
python scripts/summarise_accuracy.py v.json vr.json                              # the §8 tables
python scripts/build_check_cli.py sheets docs/BUILD_CHECK_SHEETS.md              # the bench sheets
pytest tests/test_build_check.py                                                 # 52 tests, 8 of them against ngspice
```

The results of the two accuracy runs are in `docs/build_check_accuracy_voltage_2026-10-08.json` and `docs/build_check_accuracy_voltage_ohms_2026-10-08.json`.
